passage:
"Anand, your mother says your teacher thinks you are sulking in class? Listen to your Lavanya Paati. I had the same face at your age. In our school in Madurai, I would sit very still with my face calm, like a pond, listening to every word. One day our teacher stopped the lesson and asked, 'Lavanya, why are you angry with me?' The whole class turned.
I was not angry at all! I was enjoying the story about the elephant. I said so, very softly.
She looked at me for a long moment, then smiled. 'Ah. That is just your listening face.' After that, when she wasn't sure, she asked instead of guessing.
So, tell your teacher about your listening face."

qa.q: What story was young Lavanya enjoying when the teacher stopped the lesson?
qa.a: The story about the elephant.

qa.q: What was young Lavanya actually feeling behind her calm face?
qa.a: She was interested and quietly happy listening, not angry at all; she likely felt surprised and a bit embarrassed when the whole class turned.

qa.q: What choice inside the story fixed the misunderstanding?
qa.a: The teacher chose to ask Lavanya directly and then listened to her answer, and afterwards kept asking instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt after learning it was just a listening face?
qa.a: The teacher probably felt relieved and a little sheepish for over-reading a calm face as anger.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how her calm resting face was misread as anger, showing a neutral face is not a sign of anger or disinterest.

passage:
The queue for the photo booth at the wedding snaked around the hall, and the fans barely reached it. Imran stood holding his cousin Arohi's plate while she fixed her hair for the fifth time.
"Why are you so angry?" Arohi asked.
"I'm not."
"Your face looks angry."
Imran shrugged. He wasn't smiling or frowning. He was just standing, waiting, thinking about the kebabs.
Then an aunty passed. "Imran beta, what happened? Someone scolded you?"
"No, Aunty. I'm fine. This is my waiting face."
Arohi squinted at him. "Your waiting face looks exactly like your angry face."
"My angry face has eyebrows," Imran said, and scrunched them down to show her. Arohi burst out laughing.

qa.q: What was Imran thinking about while waiting?
qa.a: The kebabs.

qa.q: What was Imran actually feeling while Arohi and the aunty kept asking?
qa.a: He felt calm and a bit bored in the hot queue, neither happy nor sad; being asked twice probably made him slightly impatient.

qa.q: What would you advise the aunty next time she sees a calm, blank face?
qa.a: Ask a light question, or simply wait, rather than assuming someone scolded the child.

qa.q: If you were Arohi, how might you tell Imran's waiting face from his angry face now?
qa.a: You might watch the eyebrows and other signs, and remember that a still face often just means waiting, not anger.

grounding: In a hot, crowded wedding queue, a child's neutral face is misread as anger, and he shows what his real angry face looks like.

passage:
On his first day teaching the evening tuition batch in Lucknow, Irfan Sir kept glancing at Ramesh. The boy sat straight, face still, eyes on the board, not smiling at the jokes.
Sir thought, He's bored. Or he doesn't like me.
When the others went out for water, Sir asked, "Ramesh, is this too easy for you? You look fed up."
Ramesh blinked. "No, Sir. I like the geometry part. I was trying to see where the angle goes."
He pointed to a line on the board. "Is it here?"
It was exactly right.
Irfan Sir laughed at himself. "I misread your face. Next time I'll just ask sooner."
Ramesh nodded, still calm, and copied the next diagram.

qa.q: What part did Ramesh say he liked?
qa.a: The geometry part.

qa.q: What was Irfan Sir feeling when he kept glancing at Ramesh?
qa.a: Sir felt unsure and a little worried, reading the still face as boredom or dislike.

qa.q: Which choice of Irfan Sir's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Ramesh directly worked, because it showed the calm face hid real interest, not boredom.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see being asked if he looked fed up?
qa.a: Ramesh was probably surprised, since he was focused and interested, and may not know his calm face gives a different message.

grounding: A new tutor over-reads a child's neutral face as boredom, then learns it hid focused interest.

passage:
During silent reading in the Madrid classroom, Alejandro turned round and made a fish face at Selin, lips pushed out, eyes crossed.
Selin pressed her lips together hard. Her shoulders shook. She bit the inside of her cheek and stared at page forty-two until the words swam. A tiny squeak escaped. The teacher looked up. Selin turned the page very seriously.
Alejandro did it again. Selin put her book in front of her face.
When the bell rang, she ran out to the yard, grabbed Alejandro by the sleeve, and they both exploded with laughter, bent double by the fence. She laughed until her stomach hurt. Then they raced each other to the goalposts and back twice.

qa.q: What page was Selin staring at?
qa.a: Page forty-two.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling while she bit the inside of her cheek?
qa.a: She felt very amused and wanted to laugh, but was working hard to hold it in because it was silent reading time.

qa.q: What made the restraint easier to keep up?
qa.a: Knowing the bell would come helped, and running out to laugh and race in the yard gave her a place to let all that energy out.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen Selin turning the page so seriously?
qa.a: The teacher probably saw a quiet reader and didn't notice the laughter being held in, except for the tiny squeak.

grounding: A child holds in laughter during silent reading using self-control, then releases it in the yard afterwards.

passage:
At the school science fair, Yash stood in line behind five other children to ask Ankita about her solar oven. He had a question burning in his mouth: would it melt chocolate?
Ankita was explaining slowly to the judge. Yash hopped from foot to foot. He opened his mouth, then closed it again. He counted the tiles on the floor.
Finally it was his turn. "Will it melt chocolate?" he blurted.
Ankita grinned. "Yes! I tested it yesterday."
Yash beamed.
After the fair, the teacher sent everyone out to the field for ten minutes. Yash ran three laps, arms out like a plane, shouting "CHOCOLATE!" at the sky.

qa.q: What did Yash count while waiting?
qa.a: The tiles on the floor.

qa.q: How can you tell Yash felt eager and impatient while waiting his turn?
qa.a: He hopped from foot to foot, opened and closed his mouth, and counted tiles, which shows eager excitement he was holding back.

qa.q: Why was the teacher's choice to send everyone to the field helpful?
qa.a: After a long time of self-control, running gave children like Yash a safe way to let out their bottled-up energy.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt answering Yash's question?
qa.a: Ankita probably felt pleased and proud that someone was so excited about her solar oven.

grounding: At a science fair, a child waits his turn with visible self-control, then gets a chance to release energy afterwards.

passage:
At our Nani's prayer meeting, the pandit's microphone suddenly made a loud squeaky noise, like a duck. Everyone kept their faces serious.
I saw my brother Uday press his lips together so tight they went white. His shoulders shook. He stared hard at the flowers in front of Nani's photo and breathed through his nose. I don't know if he was trying not to laugh or trying not to cry. Maybe both.
He managed it all through the prayers.
Afterwards, he went straight out to the garden and I followed. He laughed so hard he had to hold the gate, and then he wiped his eyes and went quiet.
I sat on the step next to him till Mummy called us for food.
- Yamini

qa.q: What sound did the microphone make?
qa.a: A loud squeaky noise, like a duck.

qa.q: What might Uday have been feeling when his shoulders shook?
qa.a: He may have been amused by the squeak and struggling not to laugh, or sad and holding back tears at the prayer meeting; Yamini can't be sure, and it may have been both.

qa.q: What helped Uday after holding it in so long?
qa.a: Going out to the garden gave him a private place to let the laughter and feelings out, with his sibling quietly beside him.

qa.q: How did Yamini experience watching Uday?
qa.a: Yamini was watching closely and caring, unsure what he felt, and chose to follow him and sit with him.

grounding: An observer watches a brother hold in laughter during a solemn prayer meeting, then release it afterwards outside.

passage:
Rafael came home from the all-day football tournament in Lisbon with mud up to his knees. He dropped his bag in the hall and didn't pick it up. He walked slowly, as if his shoes were made of stone.
His little sister Amara ran at him with her drawing. "Rafa, look! Look!"
"Not now!" he snapped, and she stepped back, lip trembling.
Their mother saw his grey face. She didn't ask about homework. "Shower, then soup, then bed," she said gently. "Amara, show him tomorrow."
After the shower Rafael sat at the table, eating slowly. Then he called Amara over. "Sorry. Show me now, quickly." He looked at the drawing and managed a tired smile.

qa.q: What did Rafael do with his bag?
qa.a: He dropped it in the hall and didn't pick it up.

qa.q: Why did Rafael snap at Amara?
qa.a: He felt worn out and drained after the long tournament, so even a small demand made him irritable rather than angry at her.

qa.q: What did the mother do that matched Rafael's weariness?
qa.a: She lowered demands by skipping homework and gave him a simple plan of shower, soup and bed.

qa.q: How might Amara have felt when Rafael snapped?
qa.a: Amara probably felt hurt and confused, since she only wanted to share her drawing.

grounding: After a long tournament, a child looks drained, moves slowly and snaps, and a parent responds with rest and low demands.

qa.q: How might Asif see Shreya's snapping?
qa.a: Asif probably felt hurt and surprised, not realising she was still tired from being sick.

passage:

passage:
On the school trip bus to the dam, it was hot and crowded, and the road wound up and down the hills. Halfway, Trisha went very pale. She clutched the seat in front.
Jagdish Sir noticed from the aisle. Was she scared of the steep drop outside the window? Feeling sick? Cold from the air conditioning?
He made his way to her. "Trisha, are you dizzy?"
She nodded, eyes closed.
He helped her sit lower, gave her his water bottle, and asked the driver to stop at the next lay-by. Outside in the shade, she sipped slowly. Colour came back into her cheeks.
"I didn't eat breakfast," she whispered.
Sir called her mother to let her know and kept her in the front seat for the rest of the trip.

qa.q: What did Jagdish Sir give Trisha?
qa.a: His water bottle.

qa.q: What was Jagdish Sir thinking when he saw Trisha go pale?
qa.a: He felt concerned and was unsure of the cause, wondering whether she was scared, feeling sick, or cold.

qa.q: What did Jagdish Sir do that was right for a pale, dizzy child?
qa.a: He had her sit, gave water, stopped the bus, and called her mother, which is the right response for sudden paleness with dizziness.

qa.q: How might Trisha have felt when the bus stopped?
qa.a: Trisha probably felt relieved and a little embarrassed to be the reason for the stop.

grounding: On a hot winding bus, a child goes pale for an uncertain reason, and a teacher has her sit, drink water and tells her parent.

On a foggy December morning at the bus stop in Delhi, Himani noticed her little brother Siddharth's face had gone white.

The maths test in the Mexico City school started right after recess. Javier slid into his seat, shirt stuck to his back, drops of sweat running down his temples.
Wei, at the next desk, whispered, "Are you okay? You look really nervous."
Javier grinned and wiped his forehead with his sleeve. "Nervous? I just ran the whole yard six times. We won the race!"
Wei looked again. Javier's face was red, not pale, and he was breathing hard but smiling. His pencil was steady.
"Oh," Wei said. "I thought it was the test."
"The test is easy," Javier said, fanning himself with the question paper. "The race was hard."
By the second question, his breathing had slowed and the sweat had dried.

qa.q: How could Wei have read the situation more accurately?
qa.a: By noticing the setting, right after recess, and other signs like a red face, a smile and a steady pencil, which point to exercise, not nerves.

qa.a: Javier seemed amused and a bit surprised, since he felt happy from the race, not worried.

qa.a: They were trembling.

qa.a: Aparna could notice other signs like trembling hands, glancing between notes and crowd, and a wobbly voice, not just the sweat.

passage:
When I was eight, our neighbour Maria Aunty came over for tea. I kept jumping on and off the sofa, running to the window, fiddling with the cushions.
Maria Aunty laughed. "Nitin, you've got ants in your pants!"
I froze. Then I checked my shorts. I even shook them a little. No ants.
She burst out laughing so hard she spilled her tea.
Mummy explained, "It's a saying. It means you can't sit still."
I felt silly, but I asked, "Why ants?"
"Because if there were ants, you'd be wriggling like that too," Maria Aunty said.
After that, I started asking whenever someone said something strange. It saved me from a lot of shaking.
- Nitin

qa.q: What did Nitin check after Maria Aunty's comment?
qa.a: The shorts.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling after checking the shorts?
qa.a: Nitin felt confused and a bit silly, having taken the saying literally.

qa.q: What habit did Nitin learn from this?
qa.a: Nitin learned to ask what someone means when a saying sounds strange, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Maria Aunty have seen Nitin checking for ants?
qa.a: She found it very funny and was amused, not meaning to embarrass Nitin.

grounding: The narrator recalls taking an idiom literally and learning to ask what someone means.

Teacher's note, Monday
This afternoon the classroom was cold because the window was open. I said, "It's a bit chilly in here, isn't it?"
Most of the class just nodded. Nitin looked at me, then at the window, and asked, "Ma'am, do you want me to close the window?"

At the boarding school, Jeevan Sir was usually cheerful at roll call. Today his voice was quieter, and he didn't crack his usual joke about the late bell.
Pranav noticed. Had he done something? Was it about the broken window in the hostel?
After roll call, Pranav hung around. "Sir, are you angry with our house?"
Jeevan Sir blinked. "No, Pranav. I have a bad toothache. It's hard to smile."
Pranav relaxed. "Oh. Sorry, Sir."
"Thank you for asking," Sir said, touching his jaw. "Better than guessing."

qa.q: What was Jeevan Sir's usual joke about?
qa.a: The late bell.

qa.q: What was Pranav worried about when he noticed Sir's quiet voice?
qa.a: Pranav felt anxious that Sir was angry about the broken window in the hostel.

qa.q: Why was Pranav's question a good idea?
qa.a: It checked the subtle cue instead of over-reading it, and cleared up the worry.

qa.q: How might Jeevan Sir have felt when Pranav asked?
qa.a: Sir probably felt touched and grateful that Pranav cared enough to check.

grounding: At a boarding school, a child notices a teacher's subtle change and checks instead of guessing.

passage:
I watched my little sister Aadhya hand Papa her report card. Papa read it, and his eyebrows went down just a little.
Aadhya's shoulders dropped. She stared at her feet.
I wasn't sure what Papa was thinking either. Maybe he was angry about the maths mark.
Then Aadhya asked in a small voice, "Papa, are you disappointed?"
Papa looked up, surprised. "No! I was just reading the teacher's comment carefully. It says you are very kind to others." He smiled and ruffled her hair.
Aadhya grinned so wide.
Next time I see Papa frown, maybe I'll ask too.
- Ujjwal

qa.q: What did the teacher's comment say about Aadhya?
qa.a: It says she is very kind to others.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when her shoulders dropped?
qa.a: Aadhya felt worried and anxious that Papa was disappointed in her.

qa.q: What did Aadhya do that cleared up the worry?
qa.a: She asked Papa directly if he was disappointed, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did Papa see his own frown?
qa.a: He was just concentrating on reading carefully, not upset at all.

grounding: An older sibling watches a child notice a parent's subtle frown, over-read it, and check by asking.

passage:
Monday: Hafsa, who helped in the school office, whispered to Omkar, "You got into the school band! But it's a secret till Friday's assembly."
Omkar's heart leapt. But he kept his face straight. "Okay," he said calmly.
Wednesday: At home, Mummy asked, "Anything new at school?" Omkar shrugged. "Nothing much." Under the table his feet were jiggling like drums.
Friday: At assembly, the principal read the names. "Omkar!" He stood up and finally let his grin burst out. He did a little jump.
Later, Mummy said, "You knew, didn't you?"
Omkar laughed. "Since Monday!"
Mummy laughed too. "You're a good secret-keeper."

qa.q: When was the band announcement?
qa.a: At Friday's assembly.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling while keeping a straight face at home?
qa.a: Omkar felt excited and bursting to share, but held it in to keep the surprise.

qa.q: What helped Omkar keep his secret?
qa.a: He kept his face calm and let out his excitement only through his jiggling feet until the right moment.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when she found out Omkar knew since Monday?
qa.a: Mummy was amused and impressed that he kept the secret so well.

grounding: Over a week, a child keeps a straight face while excited, waiting for the right moment to show it.

passage:
"Ira, you want to know how to keep a secret? Let me, your Hemant Dadu, tell you.
When I was twelve, a letter came saying I'd won a scholarship. My heart nearly jumped out of my chest! But I didn't say a word at dinner. I wanted to surprise my father after the meal.
I kept my face so serious. My mother kept looking at me. She could see my toes wiggling under the table.
After dinner, I handed Papa the letter. He read it, then laughed and hugged me. My mother said, 'I knew something was up! Your toes gave you away!'
That night, the whole family laughed. The wait made the surprise even better."

qa.q: What gave Hemant away to his mother?
qa.a: His toes wiggling under the table.

qa.q: What was young Hemant feeling while keeping a serious face at dinner?
qa.a: He felt very excited and happy, but held it in to surprise his father.

qa.q: What choice inside the story made the surprise special?
qa.a: Hemant chose to wait until after dinner to share the letter, which made the moment more exciting for everyone.

qa.q: How might Hemant's mother have felt noticing his wiggling toes?
qa.a: She was curious and amused, enjoying the delay while guessing something was up.

grounding: A grandfather recalls keeping a straight face while excited, waiting for the right moment to surprise his family.

passage:
Indu found out on the rainy school bus that she'd won the class drawing prize. Her friend had seen the list.
Her heart raced. But she kept her face calm. The last time someone won, the others teased them for being a "teacher's pet."
The bus was loud, and rain battered the windows. Indu stared outside, lips pressed together, gripping her bag.
When she got home, she burst through the door. "Vaibhav! I won! I won!"
Her brother Vaibhav looked up. "Really? You didn't look happy at the bus stop."
"I was! I just didn't want anyone to tease me."
Vaibhav laughed and gave her a high five.

qa.q: What did Indu win?
qa.a: The class drawing prize.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling while staring outside the bus window?
qa.a: Indu felt excited and happy but kept a calm face to avoid being teased.

qa.q: Why did Indu keep her face calm on the bus?
qa.a: She wanted to avoid being called a teacher's pet, so she waited to share her excitement at home.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have seen Indu at the bus stop?
qa.a: Vaibhav thought she didn't look happy, not realising she was hiding her excitement.

grounding: On a rainy bus, a child hides excitement to avoid teasing, then shares it safely at home.

passage:
In the Kerala village, Joseph was about to ride the new cycle Appachan had bought for the family. But Uncle said, "Suraj goes first. He's older."
Joseph's face tightened. He said, "Okay," through pressed lips.
Suraj rode off, grinning.
Joseph walked to the river bank and threw stones into the water, one after the other, as hard as he could. After a while, his shoulders relaxed.
Ammachi came out and sat beside him. "It's not fair, is it?"
Joseph shook his head. "I was here first."
"I'll talk to Uncle. Tomorrow, you go first."
Joseph nodded and threw one more stone, gently this time.

qa.q: Where did Joseph go to throw stones?
qa.a: To the river bank.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he said "Okay" through pressed lips?
qa.a: Joseph felt angry and treated unfairly, but held it in politely.

qa.q: What helped Joseph with his anger?
qa.a: Throwing stones at the river gave him a safe outlet, and Ammachi listened and helped fix the unfairness.

qa.q: How might Suraj see the situation?
qa.a: Suraj was probably just happy to ride first, not noticing Joseph's anger.

grounding: In a village, a child says okay politely while angry at an unfair rule, then finds a safe outlet.

passage:
At football practice in Toronto, Coach Daniel told Tariq to sit out the match. "Let others have a chance."
But Tariq hadn't missed a practice all season. He said, "Okay, Coach," through tight lips.
He sat on the bench, arms crossed, jaw clenched.
After practice, he ran three laps around the field until he was out of breath. Then he found his father in the car park.
"Coach benched me for no reason," Tariq said.
His father listened. "That sounds unfair. You were polite, and that's good. Let's talk to Coach together tomorrow."
Tariq nodded. His shoulders dropped a little.

qa.q: How many laps did Tariq run after practice?
qa.a: Three laps.

qa.q: What was Tariq feeling when he said "Okay, Coach"?
qa.a: Tariq felt angry and treated unfairly, but controlled it and stayed polite.

qa.q: What did Tariq's father do that helped?
qa.a: He listened, said it sounded unfair, praised Tariq's politeness, and offered to talk to the coach together.

qa.q: How might Coach Daniel see Tariq's tight-lipped "Okay"?
qa.a: The coach might think Tariq accepted the decision, not realising how angry he felt.

grounding: A child speaks politely while angry at being benched, then releases it through running and talking to a parent.

passage:
In the Class 6 project presentation, Farida's group had worked hard on the poster. But when the teacher praised it, she said, "Well done, Tanvir! Great work!"
Farida had drawn most of the poster. She said, "Okay, Ma'am," but her voice was tight.
After class, she went to the girls' washroom and splashed water on her face. Then she wrote in her notebook, "NOT FAIR!" in big letters.
At lunch, she calmly went to the teacher. "Ma'am, I drew most of the poster. Could you please mention the whole group next time?"
The teacher paused. "I'm sorry, Farida. You're right. I'll fix it tomorrow."
Farida smiled, relieved.

qa.q: What did Farida write in her notebook?
qa.a: "NOT FAIR!" in big letters.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when she said "Okay, Ma'am"?
qa.a: Farida felt angry and treated unfairly, but controlled it and stayed polite.

qa.q: What helped Farida handle her anger?
qa.a: Splashing water, writing in her notebook, and then calmly telling the teacher helped her release and address the anger.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel about the teacher's praise?
qa.a: Tanvir might have felt pleased but also awkward, knowing Farida did most of the work.

grounding: A child says okay politely while angry about unfair credit, then finds safe outlets and speaks up calmly.
